newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine wheat sowing seen delayed by rain.
newsitem.headline: Argentine wheat sowing seen delayed by rain.

text.p: Wet weather is still delaying 1997/98 wheat sowing in much of Argentina's grain belt, traders and analysts said Thursday.

"In general it is pretty problematic for people who haven't sown yet. Basically what has been sown is in good shape, except for in the south of Santa Fe and in Cordoba, where the drought conditions of the past two years still linger on," Ricardo Baccarin, vice-president of grain traders Panagricola Safici, told Reuters.
He said he thought about 45-50 percent of the wheat crop had been sown so far.

The government's Agricultural Secretariat said Thursday in its weekly crop report that farmers had sown 40.5 percent of an intended area of 6.5 million hectares by July 4. Farmers had sown 63.9 percent of their wheat by the same date last season, but analysts point out that 1996/97 sowing was unusually rapid.
The dryness has caused delays in Santa Fe and Cordoba, while it has rained too much in large swathes of Buenos Aires, the main wheat producing area.
It rained again in Buenos Aires Wednesday, leaving fields sodden enough to keep farmers from working for 5-10 days more, Baccarin said.

"Many producers will be worried by the delay and thinking of switching their hybrids to a longer-cycle wheat seed," he said, "In west Buenos Aires the situation is a bit worse than in the southeast. The southwest is also quite delayed."
If conditions are ideal from now on, farmers could produce as much as 14 million tonnes, Bacarrin said.
"But if this wet continues for another 10-15 days, then we'll probably cut our estimate to 13.5 million tonnes or maybe 13 million tonnes," he said.

Argentine traders say longer-term forecasts indicate the El Nino weather effect is installing itself over the country, bringing welcome snow to Andean ski centers as well as a rainy winter to the grain belt.
The bulk of analysts are betting on a crop from 12.5-14 million tonnes.

"People are definitely worried about the continued dry weather in Cordoba and Santa Fe, and worried the optimium planting date is slipping and that farmers may have to shift to shorter varieties," another analyst said.
But he pointed out that Cordoba and Santa Fe only account for a minor proportion of the wheat area.

Traders and analysts agreed that some producers in northerly crop zones will opt to skip their usual combination of early wheat and second crop soybeans this year to concentrate on the safer bet of first crop soybeans.

There was also concern that there may not be enough shorter-cycle wheat seed to go around, which could leave farmers having to sow long-cycle too late. This could mean the wheat might still be maturing when the heat of summer arrives.
Farmers sowed 7.3 million hectares with wheat last season, and produced 16 million tonnes of wheat, according to the Agricultural Secretariat.
